open-question.question: At each of the five multi-call open-question tool sites (review-milestone-requirements, the two annotating passes, the answer sweep, answer-procedure.md), where does the rule "write the full fixed command on every call, never through a variable, alias, or function" sit: once per file in the existing tool-contract sentence, repeated at every fenced call, or somewhere else in the file?
open-question.alternative: The rule goes in once per file, as a clause added to the tool-contract sentence each site already has in its opening paragraph. All five files are handled the same way, and no fenced call gets anything beside it. In review-milestone-requirements and answer-procedure.md that sentence already spells out the full command, so the clause sits right next to it. In the two annotating passes and the answer sweep, the opening paragraph names the tool without showing the command, so there the clause refers to the full command as shown in each fenced block. It is the smallest edit: one clause in each of five files. It also keeps the CLAUDE.md invariant that runtime prose states the tool's contract in at most one sentence per site, because the rule becomes part of that one sentence instead of a second statement. The rule sits far from the calls that tempt a runner to reach for a variable or function: the per-return embed, the per-block embed and lift, and the sweep's per-question loop. A runner working a later step may not have the opening paragraph in mind. In three of the five files the clause also refers to a command its own sentence never shows, and the already long contract sentence gets longer.

The rule is repeated as a short clause beside every fenced tool call in all five files, about two dozen places in total. The opening contract sentences are left as they are. The rule is in front of the runner at the moment each command is written. That holds even when the runner jumps straight into a step or re-enters a loop without rereading the opening paragraph. The same sentence appears about two dozen times. That is prose bloat, and the copies can drift apart under later edits. It also goes against the invariant of at most one contract sentence per site, so a later editor could reasonably cut the copies as redundancy. How long each clause is depends on how the host-variable wording is settled, and that is a separate question.

The rule is stated only beside the calls a run repeats: embed --alternatives once per return in the alternatives pass, embed --recommendation and lift once per block in the recommendation pass, the per-question loop in the answer sweep, remove for each question in review-milestone-requirements, and the cascade remove in answer-procedure.md. The opening contract sentences and the one-off calls (the list gathers, walk, sort, locate) get nothing. It targets the exact place this failure comes from, a runner turning a command it repeats into a variable or function, without spreading the sentence across one-off calls where nobody would be tempted. Deciding which calls count as repeated is a judgment, and it gets harder in files without an obvious loop (answer-procedure.md's single locate and remove run once per question only because a caller loops over it). One-off calls carry no rule, so a runner that sets up a variable at the first gather call is not told not to. With several mentions per file, it still goes beyond one contract sentence per site.

The rule is stated in full once per file, as a clause in the existing tool-contract sentence. Each repeated call (the per-return, per-block, per-question, and cascade calls listed in the previous option) also gets a short reminder pointing back to that clause. One-off calls get nothing beyond the contract clause. Every call in the file is covered by the general statement, and the calls where the temptation actually arises also get a reminder where they are written. The rule is in two places in every file, and that is the duplication the one-sentence-per-site invariant exists to prevent. Choosing which calls get a reminder is the same judgment as in the previous option. Each file needs the most editing under this option, and the most text has to stay consistent later.

The rule is stated once per file, as its own sentence beside the first fenced tool call in the workflow, in all five files. Examples are the first list gather in each annotating pass, the first walk in the sweep, the remove in review-milestone-requirements, and the locate in answer-procedure.md. The opening contract sentences and all later calls are left as they are. The rule is stated once per file, right next to a full written command. That fixes the contract-sentence placement's problem of a clause referring to a command its sentence does not show, without repeating the rule. The first call is usually a one-off gather. The rule then sits a step or more before the looped calls where the failure happens, so it is barely nearer the risk than the opening paragraph. Splitting the tool's contract between the opening paragraph and a workflow step also scatters something CLAUDE.md wants kept to one sentence per site.

Placement varies by file. In review-milestone-requirements and answer-procedure.md, whose tool-contract sentence already spells out the full command, the rule is a clause in that sentence. In the two annotating passes and the answer sweep, whose opening paragraph names the tool without the command, the rule is one sentence beside the first fenced call. Each file states the rule once, and nothing is added at later calls. In every file the rule is stated once and sits next to a full written command, using the existing contract sentence wherever that sentence already shows the command. The five sites are not written the same way. A later editor checking the rule has to look in two kinds of place, and one could "fix" the difference by moving the rule back into a single convention. Three files also keep a rule outside their contract sentence, which is the same distance-from-the-loop weakness the first-fenced-call option has.

open-question.question: The Claude host renders the {{PLUGIN_ROOT}} placeholder as the host-provided reference ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}, so the fixed open-question tool command as shipped there already contains one variable. How should the "never through a variable" rule be worded so that it bans variables the runner introduces itself without contradicting the command it sits beside, given that core/ files may name no host?
open-question.alternative: The rule keeps the goal's prohibition vocabulary and limits it to things the runner introduces itself. It is worded along the lines of "write the full command shown on every call; never define a variable, alias, or function of your own to stand for it or any part of it." The command it sits beside stays untouched. The sentence does not mention the plugin-root segment, and core/ prose names no host and no shell. It is the smallest change that still names variable, alias, and function, the three mechanisms the goal bans. Because the ban covers only what the runner defines, the host-provided reference in the Claude render is left out without being singled out. The wording reads the same in both rendered trees. The exemption is only implied. A runner reading the Claude render still sees "never … a variable" next to ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} and has to infer from "of your own" that the reference is allowed. Whether this one sentence fits depends on where the sibling Tool-site rule placement question puts the rule: in each file's contract sentence, or repeated at every fenced call.

The rule bans variables, aliases, and functions the runner introduces, and it also says outright that the plugin-root part of the command is written exactly as shown. That part is described by its role, not by any host's spelling. Example wording: "the plugin-root path at the head of the command is part of the fixed command and is written as shown." The rendered command stays unchanged, and core/ still names no host. It removes the apparent contradiction on the page rather than leaving it to inference. A runner looking at ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} is told directly that the reference belongs to the command and is not the kind of variable the rule bans. The sentence gets longer at every site that carries it. The Antigravity render, where the plugin root is the plain literal .agents/plugins/cairn, gets a clause about a reference that isn't there as a variable. That cuts against the CLAUDE.md rule of at most one sentence of tool contract per site. How heavy this is depends on the sibling Tool-site rule placement question.

The rule is worded only as a positive instruction to reproduce the command exactly as shown on every call, never abbreviated or rebuilt. Example: "write the command exactly as shown, in full, on every call." The words variable, alias, and function do not appear, so nothing can contradict the variable reference in the Claude render. The command and the host rendering stay unchanged. It can't contradict any host's render, because it doesn't use the vocabulary that clashes and it treats whatever the command contains as part of the fixed text. It is also the shortest wording, and it reads the same in every host tree. It drops the explicit "never through a variable, alias, or function" that the goal's text calls for, so the milestone's stated rule is only implied. A runner may not see that storing the command prefix in a shell variable and expanding it unquoted counts as not writing it out in full. That idiom is exactly the word-splitting failure this milestone targets.

The build gains a new per-host slot in scripts/hosts/<host>/settings.toml, filled into the rule sentence the same way {{PLUGIN_ROOT}} is filled now. Each host tree then gets wording fitted to its own command: the Claude host's sentence can name its plugin-root variable as the one allowed reference, and the Antigravity sentence needs no exemption at all. The core/ source carries only the placeholder and names no host. Each rendered tree reads precisely for the command it actually ships, with no inference and no clause about a reference that isn't there. The core/ rule against naming a host is kept, because the host-specific text lives in the declarative host definitions. It changes the build and its validation, which the goal doesn't ask for: a new slot constant, a fill step, unfilled-slot coverage, and a filled value in every host definition, all for one sentence of prose. It is a step toward the kind of structural fix the goal puts out of scope. It also adds a second per-host prose value that has to be kept in sync by hand.

The rule goes into runtime prose exactly as the goal words it: "write the full fixed command on every call, never through a variable, alias, or function". It has no origin scoping and no mention of the plugin-root segment. The host-provided reference is left for the runner to read as part of the fixed command. Any account of the tension goes only into the CLAUDE.md rationale, which runners in user projects never see. It adds nothing to the runtime prose beyond what the goal already specifies, so every site gets the shortest and most literal form of the stated rule. In practice the fixed command is shown right beside the rule, so the reference is plainly part of what is to be written out. On the Claude host the rule says "never through a variable" next to a command that contains one. That is the contradiction the question raises, left for each runner to resolve on its own. A literal-minded runner might try to expand or avoid ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}, which it cannot do correctly because only the host resolves that path.

Record no new bullet and leave the open-question-tool bullet and the committing bullet unchanged. The capture-milestone-principle-updates snapshot idiom (SNAPSHOT="$(mktemp)", then "$SNAPSHOT" in the copy, restore, and cleanup commands) stays exactly as it is. The idiom also keeps a separate fragility. The snapshot is set in step 6 and used in step 7 only after one or more conversation rounds, so on a host whose shell tool does not keep variables between calls, "$SNAPSHOT" expands to an empty string there: the restore cp fails and the cleanup silently leaks the temporary file.

Because runtime files carry no editor-facing prose, the capture skill's own text stays unchanged. A general rule bans variables the runner introduces in every runtime shell command, with no exception.
